CTE-NC-supporting pathologic features The same AT8 stained slides from the midfrontal, middle temporal, superior frontal, and anterior temporal tip cortices described above were used for the assessment of CTE-NC supporting pathologic features. Supporting pathologic features include characteristics of neuronal tau pathology and specific astrocytic tau pathologies (some also considered under the rubric of ARTAG). Specifically, CTE-NC-related supporting features include pattern and distribution of p-tau neuronal tangles and presence of subpial TSAs in any deep sulci. In brief, the pattern of p-tau tangles was recorded as patchy or continuous while the distribution was recorded based on whether p-tau is predominantly located either in superficial cortical layers (layers II/III) or deep cortical layers (layers IV/V) of the cerebral cortex. Participant was considered to have patchy distribution and superficial predilection of p-tau tangles if any of the cortical regions contained both cellular components. The subpial TSAs in each cortical region were recorded as present or absent in both depth of sulci and gyri as present or absent. The participant was classified as having subpial TSAs in sulci if any of the 4 cortical regions had subpial TSAs at the depth of a sulcus. We also conducted a separate assessment for the presence and the severity of perivascular p-tau astrocytes aggregates from the 4 cortical regions described above. These glial aggregates were scored separately from the CTE-NC lesion but in some cases perivascular p-tau astrocytes co-occurred with the CTE lesions. It is important to note that both subpial TSAs and perivascular p-tau astrocytic aggregates are also a component of ARTAG. ARTAG assessment ARTAG pathology including TSAs and granular fuzzy astrocytes (GFAs) was assessed from the 6 µm AT8 immunostained sections of the amygdala, anterior temporal tip, and superior frontal cortex. Each brain region was reviewed for TSA and GFA pathologies from 3 anatomical locations consisting of the gray matter, white matter, and subpial cortex ( ). In brief, a graticule was used to count the total number of each ARTAG measure in a 0.25-mm 2 highest density area (×20 magnification) from gray matter, white matter, and subpial anatomical locations of 3 brain regions. Each ARTAG measure was separately rated from 0 (none) to 5 (severe) on a 6-point scale. The overall brain ARTAG burden was defined as the highest semiquantitative measure of ARTAG burden across the anatomical location of 3 brain regions. Along with this, overall gray matter ARTAG, overall white matter ARTAG, and overall subpial ARTAG were defined as the highest semiquantitative measure of ARTAG burden across the 3 brain regions for specific anatomical locations. We also defined regional amygdala and neocortical gray matter, white matter, and subpial ARTAG. For example: neocortical gray matter ARTAG was defined as the maximum of the semiquantitative measures of ARTAG burden from gray matter location of the 2 neocortical brain regions. For descriptive statistics, a dichotomous variable present and absent was used for overall brain ARTAG as well as for overall and regional amygdala and neocortical gray matter, white matter, and subpial. For statistical models, a semiquantitative 3-level grading system (0–2) was created for overall and regional amygdala and neocortical gray matter, white matter, and subpial ARTAG burden where 0 (none, no TSAs and GFAs observed), 1 (mild); 1–5 TSAs and GFAs, and 2 (moderate-severe; 6 or more TSAs and GFAs). Because there was a minimal ARTAG burden in the white matter and subpial locations of the neocortical regions, we used a dichotomous measure (present or absent) for neocortical gray matter, white matter, and subpial ARTAG in statistical models. Subpial neocortical ARTAG is also considered under CTE-NC supporting features. PHF-tau tangles were identified by an antibody specific to phosphorylated tau, AT8 on 20-μm sections from 8 brain regions, including midfrontal, superior frontal, anterior cingulate, entorhinal, inferior temporal, inferior parietal, ad calcarine cortices, and CA1/subiculum subfield of the hippocampus. A systematic random sampling and optical fractionator probe including a counting frame of 150 by 150 µm and sampling grid of 410 by 410 µm were used to obtain an estimated quantitative measure for the total number of neurofibrillary tangle cell counts within a defined area, which was then calculated as a density measure per square millimeter ( ). Similarly, amyloid-β was identified from the same 8 brain regions mentioned above by any of the 3 antibodies using 3 monoclonal antibodies against Aβ (4G8; dilution: 1:9000; Covance Labs, 6F/3D; dilution: 1:50; Dako North America, Inc., Carpinteria, CA, and 10D5; dilution: 1:600; Elan Pharmaceuticals, San Francisco, CA). The systematic random sampling grid of 1200 by 900 µm within the Stereo Investigator software was applied to each region. A percentage of amyloid positivity was calculated using a custom positive-pixel algorithm. For analyses, the percentage of amyloid positivity was averaged across regions ( ). Because both tangles and amyloid-β measures were right-skewed, both measures were square root transformed and averaged across regions to obtain cortical amyloid-β load and PHF-tangle density. Other age-related non-AD pathologies The presence of neocortical LBs was assessed using immunohistochemistry with α-synuclein (Zymed LB 509; 1:50; pSyn, 1:20 000; Wako Chemicals) from 7 brain regions and analyzed as a dichotomous variable based on the presence in any of the assessed neocortical regions in the analyses ( ). LATE pathology was determined by immunohistochemistry using a rat phosphorylated monoclonal TAR5P-1D3 (pS409/410; 1:100, Ascenion, Munich, Germany) TDP-43 antibody. LATE-NC distribution was divided into 3 stages. In stage 1, LATE-NC was localized to the amygdala; in stage 2, there was an extension to the hippocampus or entorhinal cortex while in stage 3, there was an extension to neocortical areas. For analyses, LATE-NC distribution was dichotomized into low (none and stage 1) and high (stages 2–3) ( ). Hippocampal sclerosis (HS) was evaluated unilaterally in a coronal section of the midhippocampus and graded as absent or present based on severe neuronal loss and gliosis in CA1 and/or subiculum sector ( ). Statistical analysis McNemar tests were used to compare the fractions with CTE-NC diagnostic pathology and perivascular astrocytic tau pathology between the msTBI and matched control groups. Chi-square tests and logistic regression analyses were performed to examine the association between msTBI and CTE-NC supporting features. Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were used to compare the ARTAG pathology among msTBI and matched control groups. Other age-related pathologies including amyloid-β load, PHF-tau tangles density, neocortical LBs, LATE-NC, and HS, were compared between decedents with msTBI exposure and those without reported msTBI exposure using the Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney tests or chi-square tests. Exact 95% confidence limits are supplied for proportions. Linear regression analyses were performed to examine the association of msTBI exposure with amyloid-β load and PHF-tau tangles density and separately with phosphorylated tau peptides, while logistic regression analyses were performed to examine the association of msTBI exposure with pathologic diagnosis of AD, ARTAG, neocortical LBs, LATE-NC, and HS adjusted for demographics. All analyses were programmed in SAS/STAT version 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc., SAS/STAT 14.1 User’s Guide, Cary, NC). A nominal threshold of p < 0.05 was used for statistical significance. RESULTS One hundred eighty-eight participants, 94 with and 94 without msTBI, were included in this study. Overall, the mean age-at-death was 88.32 (SD = 7.97) years, 46% were male, 176 (93%) were non-Latino whites, 5 (3%) were non-Latino black, and 7 (4%) were Latinos. One-fourth of the participants were APOEε4 carriers, and nearly half of the participants (45%) had dementia proximate to death. Demographic and clinical, and pathological characteristics for the msTBI and non-TBI groups are summarized in . Frequency of CTE-NC in community-dwelling subjects with and without msTBI Of these 188 decedents, CTE-NC lesions were recorded in 6 decedents (point estimate = 3.2%, Exact 95% confidence interval: 1.5%, 6.8%), of whom 4 decedents had p-tau neurons around blood vessels in the depth of a sulci only, 2 had in both gyri and sulci ( ). Four of 6 decedents had multiple CTE-NC lesions and 2 had single CTE-NC lesions. The total number of CTE-NC lesions in 4 participants with multiple CTE-NC lesions is presented in . In addition, none of these decedents had neurofibrillary tangles in the cerebellum, which would have indicated a more advanced CTE-NC case. Most of the decedents had CTE-NC lesions (n = 4/6) present in the frontal region, whereas 2 brains had CTE-NC lesions in the temporal cortex without the presence in the frontal cortex. We also examined the perivascular neuronal tau severity. This characteristic is different from CTE-NC stage and does not reflect the global burden of CTE pathology. We found that more than half of the decedents (n = 4/6, 66%) had mild levels of p-tau neuronal aggregates around the blood vessel (i.e. <50% of the circumference is occupied by p-tau tangles pathology) and only 2 had moderate-to-severe p-tau neurons aggregates circumference to the blood vessel (i.e. >50% of the circumference is occupied by p-tau tangles pathology). Thus, only 2 decedents were pathologically defined as definite CTE-NC, whereas 4 were considered possible CTE-NC, after expert neuropathologist review. We also examined the demographic and clinicopathological characteristics of these 6 CTE-NC participants. The ages of the CTE-NC participants ranged from 78 to 93 years. Three out of 6 participants were diagnosed with dementia. None of the CTE-NC participants had a history of falls, a common cause of brain injury in the elderly. Specific clinicopathological information on CTE-NC participants is displayed in . Frequency of CTE-NC supporting features in community-dwelling participants with and without msTBI CTE-NC supporting features were more common in older community participants with and without msTBI than the CTE-NC diagnostic feature: 22 participants out of 188 (point estimate = 11.8%, 95% confidence interval: 7.2%, 16.4%) and 27 participants out of 188 (point estimate = 14.4%, 95% confidence interval: 9.4%–19.5%) had subpial TSAs in sulci and patchy neurofibrillary tangles in the superficial cortex, respectively. In the participants classified with possible or definite CTE-NC, all 6 brains had patchy neurofibrillary tangles with preferential locations of neurofibrillary tangles in the superficial layer cortex, although only 3 had subpial TSAs in the depth of a sulcus. All 6 CTE-NC brains also had perivascular deposition of p-tau astrocyte pathology within the area of CTE-NC lesions. Furthermore, we also observed p-tau astrocytes deposits around the blood vessel in 2 participants without perivascular p-neuronal tau. Eight participants out of 188 with perivascular astrocytic tau (point estimate = 4.3%, Exact 95% confidence interval: 2.2%, 8.2%), 6 had moderate-to-severe p-tau astrocytes circumference of the blood vessel and only 2 had mild p-tau astrocytes circumference of the blood vessel. Of these 188 participants, only 2 participants had sparse neurofibrillary tangles in the cerebellar dentate nucleus, and neither of these 2 had specific CTE-NC pathologic lesions. Frequency of ARTAG in community-dwelling participants with and without msTBI Of these total participants (n = 188), ARTAG ( ) was found in 143 brains (80%). Of these 143 brains, 137 (77%) had gray matter ARTAG, 97 (54%) had white matter ARTAG, and 92(52%) had subpial ARTAG ( ). Approximately three-fourths (n = 131) of decedents had amygdala gray matter ARTAG while more than half of subjects (n = 101) had neocortical gray matter ARTAG in either neocortical region. Of these 101 participants with neocortical gray matter ARTAG, 57 (55%) had gray matter ARTAG in only one cortical region. We also examined the distribution of TSAs and GFAs from gray matter ARTAG of both amygdala and neocortical region and found that TSAs were more common than in GFAs among all 3 regions. For example: of these 131 participants with amygdala gray matter ARTAG, 104 (79%) had TSAs without GFAs, 10 (8%) had GFAs without TSAs, and 17 (13%) had both TSAs and GFAs cell population. A similar distribution of TSAs and GFAs are seen in neocortical gray matter ARTAG. Of these 101 neocortical gray matter ARTAG, 71 (70%) had TSAs without GFAs, 12 (12%) had GFAs without TSAs, and 18 (18%) had both. Likewise, amygdala white matter and subpial ARTAG were also common, present in half of participants but neocortical white matter and subpial ARTAG was found only in a small proportion of participants, ranged from 14% to 16% of participants across regions. In all regions examined, the presence of any type of ARTAG was strongly associated with having another type of ARTAG in the same region (p < 0.001 for all). For example, the odds of gray matter ARTAG in the amygdala were 3.22 times higher than those with subpial ARTAG in the amygdala (95% CI: [2.27, 4.57], p < 0.001). The odds of gray matter ARTAG in the amygdala were 3.69 times higher than those with ARTAG in the white matter of the amygdala (95% CI: [2.59, 5.26], p < 0.001). Furthermore, the odds of gray matter ARTAG in the anterior temporal pole were 3.29 (95% CI: [1.80, 6.02], p < 0.001) and 4.78 (95% CI: [2.49, 9.19], p < 0.001) times higher than those with subpial ARTAG and white matter ARTAG of the anterior temporal tip, respectively. Similar associations were found between ARTAG types in the superior frontal cortices (p < 0.001 [all 3]). Association of msTBI with CTE-NC and ARTAG In our first set of planned analyses to examine the relationship between msTBI with CTE-NC diagnostic pathology, we found that CTE-NC diagnostic pathology was too infrequent to study discordant pairs across those with and without msTBI. Therefore, no further analytical analyses were performed. Similarly, perivascular astrocytic tau pathology was also too uncommon to examine associations with msTBI. No association was seen between msTBI and CTE-NC supporting pathology (the presence of subpial TSAs or patchy superficial distribution of NFTs) ( ). Furthermore, no associations were found between msTBI and any type of ARTAG pathologies ( ; ). Additional analyses We examined associations of msTBI exposure with several measures of PFH tau, amyloid-β plaques and other neuropathologies. Only one association was seen, with higher amyloid-β load (estimate = 0.339, SE = 0.164, p = 0.040) ( ). We ran secondary analyses by replacing the overall amyloid-β variable with diffuse and neuritic amyloid-β plaque

uncommon to examine associations with msTBI. No association was seen between msTBI and CTE-NC supporting pathology (the presence of subpial TSAs or patchy superficial distribution of NFTs) ( ). Furthermore, no associations were found between msTBI and any type of ARTAG pathologies ( ; ). Additional analyses We examined associations of msTBI exposure with several measures of PFH tau, amyloid-β plaques and other neuropathologies. Only one association was seen, with higher amyloid-β load (estimate = 0.339, SE = 0.164, p = 0.040) ( ). We ran secondary analyses by replacing the overall amyloid-β variable with diffuse and neuritic amyloid-β plaque variables. No associations were found between msTBI and diffuse and neuritic amyloid-β plaques (p < 0.05; data not shown). There were no associations seen with PHF-tau tangles, pathologic diagnosis of AD, neocortical LBs, LATE-NC, and HS ( ). The association between msTBI and tau peptides from the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in these 188 participants was also explored. Similar to PHF-tau tangles, no associations between msTBI exposure and any of the 5 phosphorylated tau peptides, including S202, T217, S262, S305, and S404 were seen ( ). DISCUSSION In 188 msTBI and matched control participants, we found that CTE-NC is an uncommon pathology in community-dwelling older persons with and without msTBI. This infrequent pathology was seen equally in persons with msTBI and persons without TBI. Pathologic features supporting CTE-NC are more common, but again are not differentially distributed across those with and without msTBI in the community. Finally, although ARTAG is very common in aging, the presence or severity of ARTAG did not differ between msTBI and the matched unexposed groups. Multiple studies have shown an association between contact sport play, as a proxy for RHI, and CTE-NC, with suggestion of a causal relationship ( ). CTE-NC has also been described in individuals with a history of RHI from military service, and other activities ( ). However, the frequency of CTE-NC in individuals with msTBI and the association of CTE-NC with msTBI remain unknown. This study systematically examined CTE-NC pathology from msTBI and matched control participants from the community and found that only a small number of participants (3%) with and without msTBI showed CTE-NC, suggesting that CTE-NC is an infrequent pathology present in community dwelling older persons and can be observed in individuals with and without a history of isolated msTBI. This finding is consistent with the other 3 community-based studies. One of these studies focused on individuals with and without TBI with LOC >1 hour ( ) while another included individuals with and without TBI, although the severity of LOC was unspecified ( ) Third, a large-scale study found no instances of CTE-NC in cases of mild TBI ( ). The infrequent occurrence of CTE-NC in a large community of individuals with a history of single episodes of msTBI is in contrasts to some ( , ) but not all studies ( , ). These mixed findings suggest caution should be used when generalizing findings from RHI to single TBI. It is also important to note that none of the CTE-NC participants in the current study had the level of pathologic changes that suggest a high CTE-NC stage, but future consensus meetings are necessary to further refine the staging criteria for CTE-NC, specifically in those with coexisting ADNC pathology ( ). Three other findings are also noted. First, we characterized the CTE-NC cases to as “possible” or “definite” based on the percentage of blood vessels circumference occupied by p-tau tangles to reflect the burden of tau tangles around the blood vessels which is different from CTE-NC stage. We found that only 2 out of 6 CTE-NC participants showed similar level of neuronal tau severity around the blood vessel that than seen in people with a history of repetitive head trauma ( , , ). The remaining 4 CTE-NC individuals do not show the same level of burden of tau tangles around the blood vessels seen in people with history of RHI. In our study, we observe that 2 out of 6 individuals with CTE-NC were female. To date, only a few studies either in contact sports or other settings have shown neuropathological findings of CTE in females ( ). This could be attributed to historical male dominance in contact sports, where head injuries are prevalent, likely contributes to the notable male bias observed in CTE prevalence thus far ( ). Since the prevalence of CTE in females remains uncertain, further research on CTE in females is necessary to gain a better understanding of potential sex-based differences in the risk of CTE-NC and its effects on behavior and cognition. Additionally, we observed that both of these female individuals exhibited CTE-NC lesions in their temporal cortex, in contrast to the other studies that highlight the frontal cortex as the initial region affected

could be attributed to historical male dominance in contact sports, where head injuries are prevalent, likely contributes to the notable male bias observed in CTE prevalence thus far ( ). Since the prevalence of CTE in females remains uncertain, further research on CTE in females is necessary to gain a better understanding of potential sex-based differences in the risk of CTE-NC and its effects on behavior and cognition. Additionally, we observed that both of these female individuals exhibited CTE-NC lesions in their temporal cortex, in contrast to the other studies that highlight the frontal cortex as the initial region affected in CTE ( , , ). The identification of CTE-NC lesions in the temporal cortex, without corresponding lesions in the frontal cortex, may however be attributed to the sampling method or a lack of examination on both hemispheres. Second, to our knowledge, we are not aware of studies that have systematically examined CTE-supporting features in participants with and without msTBI. This study not only evaluated CTE-NC diagnostic feature, but also examined CTE-NC supporting features and found that CTE-NC supporting features are relatively more common in older individuals in general, compared to CTE-NC diagnostic features, but none of the CTE-NC supporting features were related to the occurrence of msTBI. Finally, this study also examined the perivascular astrocytic tau pathology at the depth of sulci, which was considered a crucial pathology for pathological identification of CTE-NC according to the first consensus criteria ( ). However, according to the second consensus criteria ( ), perivascular astrocytic pathology deep in sulci is no longer deemed essential for recognition of CTE-NC. Nonetheless, a recent study suggests that the presence of perivascular astroglial p-tau pathology is vital for the best recognition of CTE-NC individuals ( ). We found that although perivascular astrocytic p-tau pathology at the depth of sulci is also an infrequent pathology in TBI, it is present both in all of our participants who had CTE-NC lesions (regardless of history of msTBI) and in 2 additional participants without perivascular neuronal tau. This indicates that the presence of p-tau astrocytes may be at least partially related to CTE-NC pathogenesis. Future CTE-NC studies with a specific focus on p-tau astrocytes are required to understand the significance of perivascular astrocytic tau pathology in CTE-NC pathogenesis and to determine whether the presence of perivascular p-tau astrocytic pathology could be considered a diagnostic or supportive feature for the neuropathologic diagnosis of CTE-NC. This study also provides reference data on the frequency of subpial, gray matter, and white matter ARTAG from the amygdala and neocortical regions and the relation of msTBI with ARTAG. Examination of the occurrence of ARTAG pathology at various sites in the neocortical and amygdala region suggests that ARTAG pathology occurs predominantly in gray matter followed by white matter and subpial sites in both neocortical and amygdala regions. This finding is consistent with other work that suggested a sequential pathological staging for the different ARTAG types ( ). The absence of an association between msTBI and wide spectrum of ARTAG pathologies is consistent with other studies ( , ). Nonetheless, it is worth noting that brain regions such as subcortical and brain stem as well locations such as subependymal and others were not evaluated for ARTAG pathologies. Future study encompassing a wider spectrum of ARTAG pathologies from multiple brain regions will be important to understand the connection between msTBI and ARTAG. Many clinicopathologic studies have mixed findings concerning the association of TBI with neuropathologic changes. Many studies reporting no association between TBI and AD neuropathologic changes, including CERAD score ( , ), Thal phase ( ), Braak stage ( ), and AD pathologic diagnosis ( ), while others reported higher amyloid-β load ( , ), and some others ( , ) reported higher PHF-tau tangles in those with TBI. We found higher levels of amyloid-β in individuals with msTBI, suggesting overlapping pathways between TBI and AD. Prior studies have reported that plaques seen following TBI are typically diffuse over rather than neuritic ( , ). However, we did not find an association of diffuse plaque with msTBI; this could be because of the small sample size. Further study with large number of samples is required to understand the association of msTBI with diffuse and neuritic plaques. Our study also did not find any association between msTBI and PHF-tau tangles, ARTAG pathology, and phosphorylated tau peptides. The lack of association between msTBI and tauopathies in our study highlights the heterogeneous nature of posttraumatic neuropathology and suggests that TBI-related factors like severity, frequency, and age at injury may play crucial roles in TBI and tau pathology associations. Furthermore, we observed a potential increase in the occurrence of LBs in individuals with msTBI, but the association between msTBI and LBs did not reach statistical significance. This could be because of

the association of msTBI with diffuse and neuritic plaques. Our study also did not find any association between msTBI and PHF-tau tangles, ARTAG pathology, and phosphorylated tau peptides. The lack of association between msTBI and tauopathies in our study highlights the heterogeneous nature of posttraumatic neuropathology and suggests that TBI-related factors like severity, frequency, and age at injury may play crucial roles in TBI and tau pathology associations. Furthermore, we observed a potential increase in the occurrence of LBs in individuals with msTBI, but the association between msTBI and LBs did not reach statistical significance. This could be because of limited sample size as we have found associations with LBs in our previous studies of TBI ( ). The study has several limitations. First, because msTBI relied on self-report and was solely defined by the duration of LOC, there is a possibility of misclassification for certain participants. Second, there was no information regarding exposure to RHI from contact sport participation, military service, or physical abuse. It is quite possible that brain donors with CTE-NC had RHI exposure, but did not suffer msTBI. Additionally, there was no information on age at msTBI, and the time between msTBI and death, which may influence postmortem study outcomes. Further investigation is needed to compare the relevant exposures observed in our participants with those of subsequent generations to understand how changing exposure levels may impact the risk of neuropathological outcomes. Also, we did not examine participants who report mild TBI or TBI without LOC in this study, nor did we study the relationship with tau pathology specifically ARTAG. Third, all these participants agreed to longitudinal visits and to brain donation, so they are not typical of the general population. Therefore, the frequency of CTE-NC in our community-setting samples may differ from the frequency in other populations. Fourth, given that a majority of our study participants were elderly and many of them exhibited comorbid ADNC, detection of CTE may be difficult and this could result in misclassification. In this study, unequivocal fully circumferential neuronal perivascular tau was seen in only 2 cases and more limited perivascular tau tangles noted in 4 cases with concomitant AD pathology, such that whether we include or exclude perivascular neuronal tau severity characterization, the essential findings of the study remain the same. Finally, given that msTBI can be an asymmetrical disorder and CTE and ARTAG pathology may be present elsewhere in cortical regions, by limiting the examination to one hemisphere and a small number of cortical regions, we may have underrecognized the number of cases with CTE or ARTAG. Despite these limitations, this study has some strengths. The study was conducted using a community-based design, rather than an autopsy series or clinic-based series. Our design is less prone to selection bias. Board-certified neuropathologist and trained examiners who were blinded to TBI status and demographic information performed a uniform neuropathologic evaluation for CTE-NC, ARTAG, and other neuropathologic changes. A systematic evaluation was performed not only for CTE-NC diagnostic feature, but also CTE-NC supporting features. In summary, this study demonstrates that neuropathological features of CTE are uncommon in the community and do not appear to be associated with msTBI. In addition, the significance of commonly co-occurring perivascular p-tau astrocytes in CTE-NC brains remains uncertain. Finally, ARTAG is a common age-related tauopathy in the community, but we demonstrate no association with msTBI exposure. Further studies are required to determine the relevance of astrocytic tau pathology in aging, CTE, and other dementias.

documents.title: ACSM Guidelines for exercise testing and prescription

chunks.content: Key Points Exercise has a significantly positive impact on the CRF of breast cancer survivors. MICT, M–V, HIIT, and M–V + RE had better efficacy than usual care for CRF in breast cancer survivors. Additionally, M–V + RE is significantly more effective than MICT in CRF for breast cancer survivors. M–V + RE is likely to be the optimal choice for improving CRF with the highest-ranking probability (SUCRA: 88.15%) Background Breast cancer is a major global health issue and the most prevalent cancer among women [ ]. Breast cancer has an age-standardized incidence rate of 26.88 (per 100,000) and an age-standardized mortality rate of 8.54 (per 100,000) globally in 2021 [ ]. It is projected that more than 3 million new breast cancer cases and one million deaths will occur annually by 2040 [ ]. However, improvements in early detection and treatment of breast cancer have led to side effects that put a growing number of breast cancer survivors at risk for long-term heart complications [ – ]. Breast cancer survivors are at a higher risk of developing cardiovascular disease (CVD) and CVD-related mortality compared to the general population [ – ]. A retrospective cohort study comparing CVD risk between site-specific cancer patients and noncancer controls found a substantially higher risk of CVD among breast cancer survivors (IRR, 1.13; P < 0.01) [ ]. Cancer treatment-related cardiovascular toxicity (CTR-CVT) is a growing problem in breast cancer treatment. The main clinical manifestation of cardiotoxicity is cancer treatment-related cardiac dysfunction (CTRCD). A prospective study indicated that the incidence of CTRCD among breast cancer survivors following anthracycline-based therapy was 10% [ ]. The incidence of CTRCD during or after doxorubicin treatment in this population ranged from 9 to 26%. For those receiving trastuzumab, the reported incidence of CTRCD was between 13 and 17%, while the incidence for patients receiving combined targeted and chemotherapeutic agents therapy reached as high as 27% to 34% [ ]. A study with six years follow-up period reported that breast cancer patients had a 1.77 (95% CI 1.10–2.86) times higher risk of CVD-related mortality than women without breast cancer [ ]. Another cohort study found that the most common non-cancer cause of death within 10 years after a breast cancer diagnosis were heart diseases, accounting for 15.7% of deaths [ ]. Given the available findings, exploring management strategies for cardiovascular diseases in breast cancer patients has become a research hotspot in the oncologic setting [ , ]. Cardiopulmonary fitness, an objective and integrative assessment of global cardiovascular function [ ], has been endorsed by the American Heart Association as a potentially strong predictor of all-cause mortality and cardiovascular events in healthy individuals [ – ]. In addition, mounting evidence has firmly demonstrated that CRF is also a powerful, independent predictor of cardiovascular and all-cause mortality in cancer patients [ , ]. Previous observational studies have consistently reported a reduction in CRF among breast cancer patients, who often experience impaired CRF following anticancer therapies [ , – ], and the decline in CRF may persist in breast cancer patients for up to 7 years after treatment according to previous research [ ]. A cohort study of 1632 patients indicated that the adjusted hazard ratio (HR) of cardiovascular mortality was 0.40 (95% CI 0.19–0.86) for intermediate CRF and 0.41 (95% CI 0.16–1.05) for high CRF compared with low CRF [ ]. Additionally, most of the research underpins the negative association between CRF and all-cause mortality in cancer patients [ , ]. As a robust prognosticator of cardiovascular health, CRF has been used to stratify patients according to cardiovascular risk and optimize therapeutic management strategies to reduce treatment-related adverse effects in cancer patients [ ]. Direct assessment of maximal oxygen uptake (VO 2 max) is acknowledged as the gold standard for measuring cardiorespiratory fitness [ ], and is often used to monitor fitness changes in cancer patients [ ]. A meta-analysis of 1856 breast cancer survivors suggested that VO 2 max of pre-adjuvant therapy [24.6 mL/(kg min)] was 10% [− 2.4 mL/(kg min)] higher than the VO 2 max measured after adjuvant therapy [22.2 mL/(kg min)] [ ]. Furthermore, up to 26% of patients with breast cancer had impaired VO 2 max ≤ 18.0 mL·kg −1 min −1 [ ]. Physical activity (PA) is effective in increasing VO 2 max. The American College of Sports Medicine recommends that adults engage in moderate-intensity exercise training for 30 min at least five days per week, vigorous-intensity exercise training for 20 min at least three times per week, and a series of flexibility exercises for each of the major muscle–tendon groups (a total of 60 s per exercise) at least two to three times per week [ ]. In 2020, the World Health Organization also released guidelines recommending that adults should perform 150–300 min of

≤ 18.0 mL·kg −1 min −1 [ ]. Physical activity (PA) is effective in increasing VO 2 max. The American College of Sports Medicine recommends that adults engage in moderate-intensity exercise training for 30 min at least five days per week, vigorous-intensity exercise training for 20 min at least three times per week, and a series of flexibility exercises for each of the major muscle–tendon groups (a total of 60 s per exercise) at least two to three times per week [ ]. In 2020, the World Health Organization also released guidelines recommending that adults should perform 150–300 min of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise, or 75–150 min of high-intensity aerobic exercise, or a combination of both intensities of aerobic exercise per week. In addition to this, the guidelines also recommend that adults perform regular muscle strength training and reduce sedentary behavior [ ]. Aerobic exercise promotes the release of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) through skeletal muscle contraction and its storage in platelets, which may affect cardiorespiratory fitness as they function in the body [ , ]. It has also been suggested that exercise enhances shear stress stimulation, which promotes the bioavailability of nitric oxide to restore vascular homeostasis, thereby affecting cardiovascular function [ ]. However, there are no recommended guidelines for exercise programs targeted at cardiorespiratory interventions for breast cancer survivors. Accumulated evidence supports that exercise can contribute to improving or maintaining CRF in breast cancer survivors [ , ]. PA during and after cancer treatment is safe and beneficial to improve cancer-related health outcomes in cancer patients [ – ]. It has been perceived as an important measure during cancer treatment and has been recommended in various guidelines for breast cancer treatment developed by international organizations [ – ]. Jones et al. found a significant improvement in CRF in breast cancers after 12 weeks of moderate to high intensity aerobic training compared with usual care [ ]. Moreover, the meta-analysis by Singh et al. analyzed 9 studies comprising 493 breast cancer patients to compare aerobic exercise (low to moderate intensity, vigorous intensity, continuous and interval training) with usual care and revealed a large effect in improving CRF (SMD = 1.19 [95%CI 0.45, 1.94]; p < 0.01) [ ]. However, there is no consensus on which exercise mode is the most effective for improving CRF in breast cancer survivors and how these exercise interventions rank relative to one another in terms of effectiveness [ , , ]. A recent traditional meta-analysis only compared the effectiveness of aerobic exercise with usual care, and conducted subgroup analysis between two means of aerobic exercises [ , , ]. Several RCTs have focused on the effects of combined exercise, recreational exercise and multi-component exercise on CRF in breast cancer survivors [ – ]. Direct comparisons between different intervention modalities are still lacking, but a large number of clinical trials may lead to a waste of healthcare resources. Secondary analyses using existing RCT studies may generate new research evidence and facilitate the proposal of new research directions. This may influence clinical decision-making about which exercise therapy is best for improving CRF in breast cancer survivors. Thus, a network meta-analysis (NMA) is essential. An extension of conventional meta-analysis, NMA can simultaneously compare more than two interventions, and pool the available direct and indirect evidence across multiple studies to summarize the comparative efficacy of different therapeutic options of interest [ – ]. Therefore, the aim of this study was: (1) to compare different exercise therapies simultaneously and assess their relative effects on CRF in patients with breast cancer; (2) identify the optimal choice to improve CRF in breast cancer survivors using a Bayesian network meta-analysis method. Methods Design and Registration This study has been registered at PROSPERO International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (ID = CRD42022351340). It was conducted following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses and Network Meta-Analyses (PRISMA-NMA) checklist. Literature Search The literature search for RCTs on exercise interventions for CRF in breast cancer survivors was conducted in five electronic databases from inception to October 2023, including Cochrane Library, PubMed, Web of Science, CINAHL and Embase. Moreover, a supplementary search was conducted by scanning the reference lists of relevant systematic reviews and study trials to identify eligible RCTs. A combination of Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) and free text terms, including “cardiopulmonary fitness”, “cardiovascular diseases”, “physical endurance”, “exercise”, “physical activity”, “exercise therapy”, “breast neoplasms”, “breast cancer”, “randomized controlled trial”and “controlled clinical trial”, was used as the database search strategy. The search was restricted to articles that were published in the English language. The detailed search strategies are provided in Supplementary material S1. Eligibility Criteria The studies that met the following criteria were included in the NMA: Studies: randomized controlled trials Participants: female adults with a confirmed diagnosis of breast cancer (including all stages of,

trials to identify eligible RCTs. A combination of Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) and free text terms, including “cardiopulmonary fitness”, “cardiovascular diseases”, “physical endurance”, “exercise”, “physical activity”, “exercise therapy”, “breast neoplasms”, “breast cancer”, “randomized controlled trial”and “controlled clinical trial”, was used as the database search strategy. The search was restricted to articles that were published in the English language. The detailed search strategies are provided in Supplementary material S1. Eligibility Criteria The studies that met the following criteria were included in the NMA: Studies: randomized controlled trials Participants: female adults with a confirmed diagnosis of breast cancer (including all stages of, and treatments for, breast cancer) Interventions: any type of exercise therapies with specific exercise protocols and duration of intervention ≥ 4 weeks, without a combination of other health-related non-pharmacological interventions, such as nutrition interventions Comparisons: usual care or any kind of exercise pattern different from experimental group Outcomes: outcomes of interest included maximal oxygen consumption (VO₂ max) measured directly using a cardiorespiratory exercise test or an exercise tolerance test (e.g., standard Bruce Protocol procedure). Studies were excluded if they met any of the following criteria: Participants that were focused on mixed populations or cancers other than breast cancer Full-text articles were not available and were only presented in abstract form There was a lack of complete data Studies were repeatedly published or the same subjects were used for multiple studies. Two reviewers (X. Zhou, L.W. Zhai) independently assessed the full-text articles for eligibility, and any disagreement was settled by consensus with a third reviewer (Y. Yang). Data Extraction Data extraction was performed by two independent reviewers (X. Zhou and Y. Yang), and a third author (D.F. Ding) adjudicated unresolved discrepancies. The following information was extracted from the original article: (1) study features: first author, publication year, study location; (2) sample characteristics: sample size, age, BMI and stage of treatment; (3) intervention characteristics: type, frequency, duration, intensity, and timing of exercise, other intervention-related information such as supervision and delivery setting was also extracted; (4) outcome measures: pre-intervention and post-intervention mean ± standard deviation values, or the change score before and after an intervention. Classification of Available Evidence Classification of Exercise Type We graded aerobic intensities as low, moderate, and high according to the American Heart Association equivalence table [ ] and the classification of previous studies [ – ], further, the aerobic training modes were classified as interval or continuous training. Finally, the exercise interventions included in this NMA were classified into 12 categories: (1) resistance exercise (RE); (2) stretching exercise (SE); (3) moderate-intensity continuous aerobic training (MICT); (4) moderate-to-vigorous aerobic exercise (M–V); (5) high-intensity interval training (HIIT); (6) moderate-intensity continuous aerobic training combined with resistance exercise (MICT + RE); (7) moderate-to-vigorous aerobic training combined with resistance exercise (M–V + RE); (8) high-intensity interval training combined with resistance exercise (HIIT + RE); (9) high-intensity interval training combined with moderate-intensity continuous aerobic training (HIIT + MICT); (10) YOGA; (11) multimodal exercise training (ME); (12) recreational sports (RS). Classification of Time of Exercise Onset We classified the timing of exercise intervention based on the breast cancer survivors ‘during’ or ‘after’ cancer treatment. Studies including breast cancer patients receiving chemotherapy, radiotherapy or targeted treatment as the cancer treatment were classified as ‘during’, while those studies including breast cancer survivors currently not on chemotherapy, radiotherapy or targeted treatment were defined as ‘after’. Studies including both types of subjects were classified according to the majority of subjects. Studies including patients receiving endocrine therapy without chemotherapy, radiotherapy or targeted treatment were defined as ‘after’. Risk-of-Bias Assessment and Certainty of Evidence The quality assessment was performed by two independent reviewers (X. Zhou and Y. Yang), and any conflict was resolved by arbitration with the third appraiser (C.H. Li). We appraised included studies based on the approach of “intention-to-treat” effect, using Version 2 of the Cochrane risk-of-bias assessment tool (RoB 2.0) for randomized trials. RoB 2.0 consists of five bias domains: bias arising from the randomization process, bias due to deviations from intended interventions, bias due to missing outcome data, bias in measurement of the outcome, and bias in selection of the reported result. Within each domain, one or more signaling questions are answered, resulting in a judgement of “low risk”, “some concerns”, or “high risk”, and the judgements within each domain lead to an overall risk-of-bias assessment. We also employed the Confidence in Network Meta-Analysis (CINeMA) to assess the certainty of the evidence in six key areas, including within-study bias, reporting bias, indirectness, imprecision, heterogeneity, and inconsistency. Then, CINeMA assigns judgments at 3 levels (no concerns, some concerns, or major concerns) to each domain. Judgments across domains can be summarized to obtain 4 levels of confidence for each relative treatment effect, corresponding to the usual GRADE assessments of very low, low, moderate, or high. Data Synthesis R Version

“low risk”, “some concerns”, or “high risk”, and the judgements within each domain lead to an overall risk-of-bias assessment. We also employed the Confidence in Network Meta-Analysis (CINeMA) to assess the certainty of the evidence in six key areas, including within-study bias, reporting bias, indirectness, imprecision, heterogeneity, and inconsistency. Then, CINeMA assigns judgments at 3 levels (no concerns, some concerns, or major concerns) to each domain. Judgments across domains can be summarized to obtain 4 levels of confidence for each relative treatment effect, corresponding to the usual GRADE assessments of very low, low, moderate, or high. Data Synthesis R Version 3.5.1 and GeMTC software were utilized to implement this NMA [ ]. All data analyses were conducted under a Bayesian random-effects model supported by the R “gemtc” and “rjags” packages [ ]. The Bayesian approach offered probabilistic distributions of the estimates of each effect by simulating the posterior distribution of the parameters, using the Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method [ – ]. We set a total of 25,000 tuning iterations and 250,000 simulations with a thinning factor of 10 to generate the Bayesian statistical model for this NMA. Inconsistency was checked using consistency and inconsistency models. As closed loops were found in the network graph, a node-splitting method was planned to assess the local inconsistency between direct and indirect evidence [ ]. The achievement of convergence was appraised using the Brooks-Gelman-Rubin diagnostic tool combined with visual inspection of trace plots and density plots. Effect sizes were estimated with mean differences (MDs) and 95% credible intervals (95% CrIs) by a Bayesian random-effects model. Results of comparisons between all interventions were presented in a forest plot and league table. The comparisons were considered statistically significant when the 95% CrIs did not include the value of 0 effect. We created the distribution of probability for ranking exercise therapies for efficacy outcome and calculated the surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA) to hierarchize these interventions. SUCRA values range from 0 to 100%, with higher SUCRA values indicating a greater likelihood that a therapy is superior [ , ]. The network geometry diagram was constructed to display the relative relationship between the various exercise interventions in this NMA, in which the nodes represent each type of exercise intervention and the edges correspond to direct head-to-head comparisons between interventions. Furthermore, network meta-regression analysis (during and after cancer treatment) was conducted using the mtc.model function from the gemtc R package, to evaluate if the timing of exercise intervention has an influence on the effects in our network meta-analysis. The covariate was considered to have indeed affected the NMA results when the 95% CrI of regression predictor B did not include zero. A comparison-adjusted funnel plot was created for evaluating the publication bias or small sample size effects. Results Literature Search A total of 3732 records were initially retrieved. We reviewed 298 full-text articles for eligibility after removing the duplicates and screening the titles and abstracts. Forty-one RCTs that met the selection criteria were included in this NMA. Reasons for exclusion (n = 257) are provided in Fig. . Characteristics of the Included Studies The characteristics of the included studies are illustrated in Table . A total of 41 studies with 2606 subjects were included in the NMA. Among the included studies, 29 were two-arm trials and 12 were three-arm studies. From these 12 three-arm studies, we extracted the data from the intervention of interest (two arms) in four studies for the current NMA. Twenty-one studies clearly reported allocation concealment, while fifteen studies did not provide relevant information in this regard. Most studies were analyzed based on the intention-to-treat principle; 17 studies had lost outcome data for more than 5% of participants. Among the 41 studies, only 11 studies (26.8%) clearly described the blinding process of outcome assessment, while 26 studies (63.4%) did not report blinding of outcome assessors. The outcome assessors were aware of the intervention received by study participants in four studies. The bias in measurement of the outcome depends on whether the measurement of outcome is subjective or objective, rather than blinding of the assessors according to the RoB 2.0 criteria [ ], and included studies of this NMA used cardiopulmonary exercise testing (the gold standard) or submaximal exercise testing as the objective assessment to determine VO₂ max [ ]. Therefore, a low risk of bias was still considered present in the domain of measurement of outcomes despite the assessors responsible for evaluating the outcome not being blinded in most studies. Overall, 17 (42.5%) were deemed to have a low risk, 19 (47.5%) raised some concerns, and 5 (10%) were categorized as having a high risk. The CINeMA ratings of mixed evidence are shown in Fig. , and the certainty of indirect evidence can be found in Supplementary material S2. Our confidence in effect estimates of M–V is high certainty, the effects of M–V + RE is moderate, and the effects of MICT and HIIT are low certainty when compared to usual care. Overall certainty of evidence varied from ‘very low’ to ‘high’, and most of the results were of moderate or low confidence. Our main reasons for downgrading were study limitations due to high risk of bias and imprecision. Discussion We conducted the first NMA to explore the comparative efficacy of 12 exercise interventions for improving CRF in breast cancer survivors. The results indicated that MICT (MD: 1.6, 95%CrI 0.13 to 3.1; low certainty), M–V (MD: 3.4, 95%CrI 1.9 to 5.0; high certainty), HIIT (MD: 2.9, 95%CrI 1.2 to 4.6; low certainty), and M–V + RE (MD: 4.3, 95%CrI 2.5 to 6.1; moderate certainty) all significantly improved CRF compared to usual care, and M–V + RE had better efficacy in improving CRF compared to MICT (MD: 2.7, 95%CrI 0.4 to 5.0; low certainty). In addition, our analysis showed that M–V + RE is likely to be the optimal choice with the highest cumulative probability (SUCRA = 88.15%) in terms of improving CRF in breast cancer survivors, followed by HIIT + MICT (SUCRA = 79.69%), M–V (SUCRA = 76.48%), and then by HIIT (SUCRA = 65.84%). Our findings align with several previous studies showing that exercise has a significantly positive impact on the CRF of breast cancer survivors [ , , ]. A meta-analysis by Scott et al. including 48 randomized controlled trials, observed that exercise was associated with a significant increase in CRF (+ 2.80 mL/kg/min) compared with no change (+ 0.02 mL/kg/min) in the control group (P < 0.001) [ ]. Similarly, Tsai et al. found that exercise significantly improved CRF in breast cancer survivors measured by VO 2 max (SMD 1.79, 95% CI 0.99–2.59) when compared to usual care [ ]. Physiologically, previous studies demonstrated that exercise can induce favorable adaptations to the cardiovascular system including physiological remodeling of the heart with the manifestation of an increase in O 2 consumption, improvement of cardiac contractile function, increased muscle oxidative capacity and improved vascularization and mitochondrial enzyme function [ , ]. In terms of survival, cardiorespiratory fitness is inversely associated with all-cause, CVD and cancer mortality in cancer patients [ , ]. In this context, Peel et al. observed that women with moderate and high CRF had a 33% and 55% lower risk of dying from breast cancer, respectively [ ]. In cohort studies of 2973 patients with nonmetastatic breast cancer, engaging in 11 to 24.5 MET-h/wk and > 24.5 MET-h/wk resulted in risk reductions of 21% (HR: 0.79; 95% CI 0.66–0.96) and 35% (HR: 0.65; 95% CI 0.53–0.80) for developing cardiovascular event [ ] In addition, CRF is directly related to quality of life in breast cancer survivors [ ]. Given the clinical importance of exercise in cancer patients, oncology care teams are increasingly calling for the incorporation of exercise into oncology care [ , ] The clinical effect of exercise for physical and psychological health differs in parameters, including type, intensity, amount, mode of exercise, and timing, which are crucial for designing effective exercise schemes [ ]. Given the clinical importance of exercise in cancer patients, oncology care teams are increasingly calling for the incorporation of exercise into oncology care [ , ] The clinical effect of exercise for physical and psychological health differs in parameters, including type, intensity, amount, mode of exercise, and timing, which are crucial for designing effective exercise schemes [ ]. At present, however, no comprehensive study has investigated the relative effects of exercise mode and intensity on CRF in patients with breast cancer. Therefore, we performed a Bayesian NMA of multiple studies to determine the optimal type and intensity of exercise to effectively improve CRF for breast cancer survivors. As compared with previous work, we further classified the exercise therapies according to intensity, interval or continuous nature, and mode (with or without resistance training), then we individually appraised each exercise type and compared all available exercise types simultaneously using Bayesian NMA [ ]. The findings of our study showed that MICT, M–V, HIIT, and M–V + RE all significantly improved CRF compared to usual care, and M–V + RE showed a non-significant increase compared to HIIT (MD: 1.39, 95%CrI − 1.0 to 3.9). Similarly, compared to MICT, HIIT showed clinical improvements in CRF, although there was no statistical significance (MD: 1.28, 95%CrI −0.7 to 3.3). Furthermore, we observed that M–V + RE had better efficacy in improving CRF compared to MICT (MD: 2.7, 95%CrI 0.4 to 5.0). These findings provide new insights into the choice of exercise prescriptions for improving CRF in breast cancer survivors, and can be utilized to make evidence-based decisions appropriately based on a comprehensive consideration of factors including clinical efficacy of exercise schemes, patient preferences, tolerance of intensity, cancer-related fatigue, time restrictions and cost-effectiveness [ , ]. Previous studies reported that the majority of breast cancer survivors do not follow the physical activity recommendations [ , ]. The studies indicated that a commonly mentioned physiological barrier to physical activity is cancer-related fatigue in cancer patients [ , ]. It is interesting that Brooke et al. found fatigue was a determinant of intervention adherence among participants randomized to high-intensity interval training [ ]. There is mounting evidence that breast cancer chemotherapy protocols elicit high levels of fatigue (ranging from 60 to 90%) [ , ], which can greatly decrease a patient’s ability to maintain a target intensity. This is particularly important since a lack of adherence or exercise training cessation may lead to detraining effects [ , ]. An optimal exercise prescription requires balancing patients'tolerance with an exercise dose that has cardioprotective efficacy. Accordingly, MICT may be preferable to HIIT for some breast cancer survivors undergoing chemotherapy who would likely not tolerate high intensity, although several studies showed HIIT appears to display comparable to or even more significant benefits than MICT on CRF [ , , ]. For breast cancer survivors who have returned to work or family, there is also a challenge to get them engaged in physical activity. This group complained that “lack of time” was the main barrier to exercise adherence, mainly because of work restrictions, childcare commitments, commuting and social activities [ ]. Therefore, from a time-pressure perspective, HIIT, which is generally considered a time-efficient training [ ], is a viable alternative when cancer patients can adapt to a high-intensity interval mode. In addition, we ranked the interventions to identify superiority by estimating the surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA). The value of SUCRA ranges from 0 to 1, with higher values denoting a greater likelihood to be in the top rank or highly effective. Our analysis showed that M–V + RE seemed to be the optimal choice with the highest probability (SUCRA = 88.15%) in terms of improving CRF in breast cancer survivors, followed by HIIT + MICT (SUCRA = 79.69%), M–V (SUCRA = 76.48%), and then by HIIT (SUCRA = 65.84%). Based on existing studies in cancer patients, M–V + RE is more frequently included in clinical trials of cancer patients (8 out of 41), and, indeed, is reported to have a good adherence rate [ , , ]. Based on these findings and the results of previous studies [ ], initiating a progression of M–V + RE can be recommended as the primary choice to improve CRF in breast cancer survivors. However, caution should be exercised when interpreting the results of the ranking probability, as HIIT + MICT tended to improve CRF in breast cancer survivors compared with usual care (MD: 4.3, 95%CrI − 0.45 to 9.0), although no significant difference was found. This could be attributed to the limitation of weak evidence i.e. only one study provided data for HIIT + MICT in our NMA. M–V + RE can be recommended as the primary choice to improve CRF in breast cancer survivors. However, caution should be exercised when interpreting the results of the ranking probability, as HIIT + MICT tended to improve CRF in breast cancer survivors compared with usual care (MD: 4.3, 95%CrI − 0.45 to 9.0), although no significant difference was found. This could be attributed to the limitation of weak evidence i.e. only one study provided data for HIIT + MICT in our NMA. Further research is needed to provide more evidence about the optimal exercise modalities. Many researchers have been focused on a "hot" and interesting topic in cardio-oncology, regarding the best time of exercise onset for women with breast cancer, but the most appropriate timing remains unknown [ , , , ]. The findings of our network meta-regression analyses suggested that the covariate of “exercise intervention during or after cancer treatment” did not appear to significantly influence the relative efficacy of exercise compared to usual care. Our findings support previous studies in breast cancer survivors, which directly compared the effects of different timing of exercise on improving CRF [ , ]. Vincent et al. explored the impact on CRF of a home-based PA program during or after specific cancer treatment in a 3-arm study, and reported the between-group difference in VO 2 max observed 12 months after the beginning of the trial was not significant [ ]. Another study by Scott et al. also found that no statistical difference in CRF improvement was observed between concurrent vs. sequential exercise therapy relative to usual care in women with primary breast cancer ( P = 0.48) [ ]. These research findings might deviate from the researchers’ hypotheses that the outcomes may differ as a function of when the exercise intervention begins, due to the existence of physiological differences exhibited by breast cancer survivors during and after treatment [ , , ]. The discrepancy between research results and hypotheses may be explained by the scarcity of studies directly comparing the effects of different timing of exercise on CRF improvement [ , ]. Clearly, the research findings from a few studies are not conclusive. Therefore, further studies will be necessary to continue to explore the relative effect of exercise for improving CRF in breast cancer survivors before, during, and after cancer treatment, accumulating sufficient evidence for providing specific exercise recommendations to breast cancer survivors during or after cancer treatment. To increase comparability across future studies, we believe that several aspects need to be considered in the study design: (1) the same volume of exercise, because two variables were mixed in previous studies, timing of onset and duration of exercise, which introduces a bias in interpretation of the results [ ]; (2) the same setting and patient cohort, which can ensure that the effects of different timing of exercise on CRF improvement can be compared directly; (3) observing the long-term benefits of exercise in improving CRF, as the improvement in VO 2 max obtained after exercise was found to be maintained [ ]. Although we identified eight closed loops in our NMA, the majority of the included studies (28 out of 41) compared single exercise intervention with usual care, and lacked head-to-head comparisons among different exercise types. Furthermore, many studies included in this NMA (22 out of 41) had small sample sizes with less than 50 subjects. Hence, the results obtained from our Bayesian NMA should be interpreted with caution and may not provide definitive conclusion. To strengthen the evidence base, we recommend conducting more large-scale clinical studies of head-to-head comparisons among various exercise interventions in breast cancer survivors. Strengths and Limitations This is the first Bayesian NMA focusing on the improvement of CRF in breast cancer survivors. It successfully integrates direct and indirect evidence from all eligible RCTs to estimate the comparative efficacy of multiple exercise interventions for improving CRF, offering more data on the different exercise prescriptions, including intensity and mode to achieve the larger CRF improvements. Methodologically, our NMA employed a Bayesian framework. The use of a Bayesian approach could overcome a shortcoming of frequentist methods that 95% CIs of effect estimates cannot be interpreted in terms of probabilities [ ]. Furthermore, the Bayesian framework has other advantages including the straightforward way to make predictions and the possibility of incorporating different sources of uncertainty [ ]. The present Bayesian NMA also has certain limitations. First, NMA relies on the assumption of transitivity, which assumes that the trials included in the analysis are comparable in terms of patients and characteristics. Although our NMA model consistency holds, heterogeneity may arise from factors such as age, disease stage, duration of intervention, and the CRF assessment method [ , ]. The present Bayesian NMA also has certain limitations. First, NMA relies on the assumption of transitivity, which assumes that the trials included in the analysis are comparable in terms of patients and characteristics. Although our NMA model consistency holds, heterogeneity may arise from factors such as age, disease stage, duration of intervention, and the CRF assessment method [ , ]. Therefore, while the results of the NMA provide valuable insights, they should not be considered definitive conclusions. To further validate these findings, it is necessary to conduct more high-quality RCTs with larger sample sizes in the future. Moreover, we did not further classify the group according to the timing of interventions, since the goodness-of-fit of the models was not satisfactory. This could be attributed to large heterogeneity in intervention characteristics. Finally, it is important to note that our NMA focused on investigating the efficacy outcomes and did not include a synthesized analysis of safety data and treatment compliance when analyzing the probability ranking of exercise therapies. This is because some of the included RCTs did not report adverse effects or attendance rates, which limits our comprehensive understanding of the safety profile and patient adherence to the exercise interventions, but would be worth exploring in future studies. Conclusions The findings of our study contribute to the evidence of the benefits of MICT, M–V, HIIT, and M–V + RE as available options for improving CRF in breast cancer survivors, and M–V + RE may be the optimal choice. However, more large and higher-quality studies of head-to-head comparisons among exercise interventions will be necessary to verify these findings of our NMA. Key Points Introduction Physical activity undisputedly offers widespread benefits across all age groups and sexes, including preventing and treating chronic diseases [ , ]. The World Health Organization currently recommends 150–300 min of moderate-intensity exercise at least 5 days per week or 75–150 min of high-intensity exercise at least 3 days per week; the more, the better [ , ]. However, individuals with underlying or undiagnosed medical conditions, especially those who engage in sudden, high-intensity exercise, may face health risks, including musculoskeletal injuries and, more rarely, serious cardiac events [ – ]. This phenomenon, often called the “exercise paradox”, highlights that while exercise reduces long-term cardiovascular risk, it can also trigger acute cardiac events in vulnerable individuals [ ]. A sports preparticipation evaluation (PPE) is recommended to mitigate such risks by identifying at-risk individuals and providing guidance on safe physical activity [ ]. To date, most international recommendations for PPEs have focused on elite athletes and are primarily based on expert consensus derived from organized competitive sports, such as the current European Federation of Sports Medicine Associations (EFSMA) guideline on preparticipation medical evaluation for elite athletes [ ]. The Italian Working Group has recently updated the Italian Cardiological Guidelines (COCIS) for Competitive Sport Eligibility in athletes with heart disease [ ]. Only few guidelines have specifically addressed recreational athletes or individuals who are new or returning to exercise [ ]. In this context, the American College of Sports Medicine (ACSM) proposed a two-stage screening process before the start of moderate or intense training [ ]. The European Association for Cardiovascular Prevention and Rehabilitation (EACPR) [ ] has also introduced screening guidelines for middle-aged and older adults before exercise that vary according to the individual’s cardiac risk profile and the intended level of physical activity. Ermolao et al. [ ] compared the EACPR and ACSM guidelines [ , ], finding that 49% of cardiovascular conditions were missed by the EACPR guidelines, 29% by the older ACSM guidelines, and 50% by the new ACSM guidelines. Therefore, the most effective and practical methods of evaluating sports-related risks in apparently healthy adults (aged ≥ 18 years) who are starting or resuming intense physical activity remain to be identified. To address this need, a consensus-based guideline was developed under the auspices of the German Society for Sports Medicine and Prevention (Deutsche Gesellschaft für Sportmedizin und Prävention [DGSP]) [ ]. This guideline is based on current international recommendations and is aimed at healthy adults, including individuals recovering from conditions such as cancer, joint injuries, or joint surgeries—not elite athletes. The PPE should be performed by specialized sports physicians who are adequately trained in the cross-disciplinary nature of the evaluation (for specialist medical training see European Union [EU] Article 26 of Directive 2005/36/EC [ ] or course-based medical training in sports medicine, Germany [ ]). The PPE may also serve as a baseline for exercise-related counseling, applying the frequency, intensity, time, type, volume, and progression (FITT-VP) principle. In addition, the individual’s cardiorespiratory and muscular fitness should be assessed owing to their protective nature against noncommunicable diseases [ , ]. The aim of this paper was to provide an overview of the consensus-based guidance that was published on the Guidance Manual of the German Association of Scientific Medical Societies (Arbeitsgemeinschaft der Wissenschaftlichen Medizinischen Fachgesellschaften [AWMF]) register [ ] and to contextualize the recommendations for an international audience. In addition, we summarized the approach and methods employed and provided further detail of the screening algorithm, background considerations underlying each recommendation, resp. medical history and examination forms. Methods The DGSP, a nonprofit specialty organization, commissioned this consensus-based guideline. It was developed on the basis of the Guidance Manual of the German Association of Scientific Medical Societies (Arbeitsgemeinschaft der Wissenschaftlichen Medizinischen Fachgesellschaften [AWMF]) and followed the process outlined in Fig. . Guideline Classification German clinical practice guidelines are developed with a classification system (S-classification) that describes how much systematic methodology is applied [ ]. The guideline classes range from S1 (recommendations by expert groups, developed using informal consensus) to S2e (evidence-based guidelines without formal consensus methods) and S2k (formal consensus-based guidelines without systematic evidence reviews) to S3 (formal consensus-based guidelines with systematic evidence reviews). The developing organization chooses the class according to how much effort is appropriate and feasible. The DGSP was responsible for the guideline development and selected class S2k. Therefore, the development of this guideline involved a formal, structured consensus process within a representative committee but no systematic review of the evidence. We suspected that comparative studies could not adequately address many of the clinical questions for a guideline on sports PPEs (see Sect. ). Therefore, the development of an evidence-based guideline would be neither feasible nor resource-efficient at this stage. Stakeholder Involvement All relevant professional groups, including specialist societies and organizations, appointed delegates to the Guideline Development Group (Box 1). The DGSP’s executive and scientific advisory boards nominated a panel of 14 experts to support the development of recommendations in an advisory capacity; panel members were selected for their expertise in various specialist areas (e.g., sports cardiology, orthopedics, ophthalmology, and neurology). The views and preferences of the target population (i.e., potential participants) and the target users of the guideline (i.e., sports physicians and general practitioners) were collected with two online surveys [ ]. The surveys addressed the acceptability and feasibility of the PPE, and respondents were asked to comment directly on the draft recommendations. Their feedback informed discussions about the final recommendations and remarks on views and preferences that were added to the complete guideline text. Management of Competing Interests All authors of the guideline disclosed any direct, financial, or indirect interests using an online form. A peer group assessed the relevance and level of conflict indicated before the consensus conference (Supplementary Material 1). Systematic Review of Existing Guidelines and Recommendations In preparation for guideline development, we systematically reviewed the evidence- or consensus-based recommendations for PPEs published since 2012 [ ]. This review was intended to identify potential guideline questions and determine the availability of primary study evidence to support the PPE recommendations. It resulted in 35 guidelines and consensus statements identified from developed countries worldwide (Fig. ). These mainly targeted athletes or participants in organized sports but some targeted the general population or specific subgroups. A total of 305 recommendations were made over various topics. Most recommendations (87%) did not cite evidence from primary studies. Guideline Questions On the basis of the systematic review (Sect. ), the steering group proposed guideline questions [ ] that were revised, discussed, and finalized in an online Delphi process, including a survey and consensus meeting [ ]. Evidence Base The systematic review (Sect. ) was used to obtain evidence from primary studies as follows. Whenever the 35 selected guidelines and consensus documents (Supplementary Material 2) directly linked their recommendations to primary studies, these were used as evidence for our guideline (55 studies; Fig. D). However, most included documents were consensus-based and did not refer to primary studies as evidence. Therefore, the evidence base was supplemented with comparative studies of PPEs that were known to the authors of this German guideline or recommended for consideration by the participating experts. The German S2k class of guidelines does not generally entail a full systematic review of primary studies, and no such review was conducted (see Sect. for the rationale). Each guideline was appraised using Domains 3 (“Rigour of Development”) and 6 (“Editorial Independence”) of the Appraisal of Guidelines for Research and Evaluation-II (AGREE-II) [ , ]. Each primary study was assigned a level of evidence [ ]. Development of the Recommendations The delegates and experts formed three working groups for internal medicine, orthopedics, and other topics. Each working group reviewed the relevant primary evidence and prepared draft recommendations on the basis of the guideline questions. They reviewed the results of the stakeholder surveys, revised the recommendations, and wrote background text explaining the rationale for each recommendation. Strength of the Recommendations The Guideline Development Group determined the strength of recommendations through a formal consensus procedure. Symbols and specific wording were used to express the grade of recommendation as defined in the AWMF Guidance Manual (Table ) [ ]. This table also indicates the corresponding class under the American College of Cardiology (ACC)/American Heart Association (AHA) Clinical Practice Guideline Recommendation Classification System that is widely used by organizations such as the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) [ ]. The grading corresponds to the degree of certainty that the observed benefit of an intervention outweighs its potential harm and that the positive effects are relevant to the guideline population. When grading the recommendations, we considered the balance of benefit to harm, benefit to estimated cost, confidence in the evidence (where available), potential participants’ survey-reported views and preferences, sports physicians’ survey-reported perceptions of feasibility, and the Guideline Development Group’s clinical expertise.
